description: pkey-peer/1 byte-level rules (WIRE-CONTRACT-V5 sections 15.4 to 15.7 and 15.9; plans/CC-01-cloud-connect.md 2.4, 2.6, 2.7, 2.9). Hex fields are lower-case. `adverts`: `names` (the mode-a instance: p1- and the first 16 characters of the lower-case RFC 4648 base32, no padding, of HMAC-SHA256(K_disc, 'pkey-peer/1 disc' || 0x00 || u64be(epoch) || the 24 device-id bytes)), `epochs` (now / 900), `tags` (the h value), `txt` (TXT parsing), `instances` (the name shape) and `browse` (which roster device an instance belongs to); `prologue`; `psk`; `sas` (the code with its commit and reveal rows); `frames` (TCP framing); `records` (flags, MORE, the critical and mode rules, the 1 MiB limit); `relayEnvelopes`; `handshakePayloads`; `lanAddresses` (which peer addresses a device dials or accepts, and the per-address count key); `mdnsAnswers` (which A and AAAA records a browser believes); `vouch` (the mode-v vouch of 15.6.1: `requests`, `results`, `flows`, `finish`); `contact` (inter-account links, 15.10: `secrets`, `bodies`, `categories`, `exchange`, `store`, `listener`, `pin`, `adverts`, `rooms`, `tickets`); `xfer` (Direct Transfer, 15.11: `codecs`, `window`, `offer`, `hash`, `ending`, `resume`, `name`, `limits`); `local` (account-free local pairing, 15.12: see its own note); mode c also adds rows to `prologue` and `handshakePayloads`. A device id is 32 base64url characters and is hashed and sent as its 24 decoded bytes. The device proof is device-proof.json. Append-only: a new row keeps peerMatrixVersion; a changed row or rule bumps it.

sas.note: h is the 32-byte Noise handshake hash. code = u32be(HKDF-SHA256(salt = h, ikm = nD || nM, info = 'pkey-peer/1 sas' || 0x00 || mode)[0..4]) mod 10^6, shown as six digits with leading zeros and a space between the triples. A nonce and a commitment travel as 43 base64url characters; the body of SAS_COMMIT is the compact JSON object with the member c, SAS_NONCE nM and SAS_REVEAL nD. c = SHA-256(nD).

frames.note: A frame is u16be len || Noise message, len 1..65535. `decode` reads a byte stream: it returns the complete frames and the unread rest; a zero length closes the session with peer_bad_frame, wherever it occurs.

records.note: A Noise transport plaintext is u16be type || u8 flags || body. Flag bit 0 is MORE; any other bit closes with peer_bad_frame. A body is {fill, count} (one hex byte repeated) where it is large. `types` is the type table; a type outside it is unknown, critical when bit 0x8000 is set. In `sessions` each record is read in order and `at` is the 0-based index of the record that closed the session. Checks run per record: flags, then a continuation of another type (peer_bad_frame), then the type (unknown critical, mode), then the running size over 1 MiB (peer_bad_frame), then, on the last record of a chain, a fixed body length (peer_bad_frame). An unknown non-critical type is dropped, MORE chain and all. delivered lists the reassembled messages as type, length and SHA-256.

relayEnvelopes.note: One binary WebSocket message is an envelope: op byte, then the layout of 15.7. A device is its 24 decoded device-id bytes. MEMBERS carries the count n as one byte; PONG echoes the 8 bytes of the PING it answers. `dir` is the sender: toRoom (a client to the room) or toClient. `messages` encode and decode both ways; `refused` rows decode to nothing; `sizes` rows are an op, a 24-byte device, a session and a run of `fill` bytes up to `total` bytes, whole. A message over 65,564 bytes is refused.

handshakePayloads.note: Handshake payloads (15.5): strict JSON of 15.1/1.2, an object, at most 8 KiB of UTF-8. Message 1 needs v = 1 (the integer token: 1.0 and 1e0 are refused) and no cert; messages 2 and 3 need v = 1 and caps (at most 32 entries matching ^[a-z0-9]+/[0-9]+$). Mode a adds cert (a non-empty string; its verification is cases.json peerCertCases) and ring (an integer token from 1 to 2^53 - 1); modes v and p refuse a cert. Unknown members are ignored. `payload` is the text, `payloadHex` the raw bytes where the text is not valid UTF-8, `payloadPad` the text prefix + count x fill + suffix. `want.caps` is the list as sent; the session uses `intersection`: the entries both lists hold, once each, in byte order.

lanAddresses.note: LAN addresses (15.4.1): lanVerdict(remote, local, allowLoopback) -> {dial, key}, applied to an accepted socket before it takes a slot or is read, to a dialled address's text before connect and again to the connected socket before its first byte. `remote` is the socket's peer address as text and `local` its own address (absent: unknown). Spelling: a zone is `%` and 1 to 15 characters of U+0021 to U+007E other than `%`; an empty or longer zone, a second `%`, a control, a space or a non-ASCII character, a zone on IPv4 and a zone on an IPv4-mapped address are malformed and refused; the grammar is strict (RFC 3986 IPv4address and IPv6address): no whitespace, NUL, port, prefix length, trailing dot, brackets, non-ASCII digits or leading-zero octet. IPv4-mapped (::ffff:0:0/96) is judged as its IPv4 address. IPv4: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, and 127/8 only with allowLoopback. IPv6: fe80::/10; fc00::/7, which with a known `local` must be IPv6 (not mapped) in the same /64; ::1 only with allowLoopback; an address in 2000::/3, outside 2001::/32 (Teredo) and 2002::/16 (6to4), only when `local` is IPv6 (not mapped) in the same /64. Anything else, and text that is not an address, is refused. `key` is the per-address connection count key: dotted IPv4, or RFC 5952 lower-case IPv6 text without its zone, except that a link-local (fe80::/10) key keeps its zone; null when `dial` is false. `group` is the per-group count key of a key: `fe80::/10%zone` for a link-local key (`fe80::/10` with no zone), `a.b.c.0/24` for an IPv4 key, `<masked address>/64` for any other IPv6 key, and null for no key. `candidates` holds the rule for a CANDIDATES entry (15.6).

candidates.note: CANDIDATES entries (15.6, 15.4.1): candidateTarget(entry, interfaces) -> {host, port} or null. `interfaces` lists the device's own addresses, one per entry: `{address, prefix, up, tunnel}`, `tunnel` meaning a VPN, tunnel, point-to-point or pseudo-interface. An entry is dialled only when all hold: it is `a.b.c.d:port` or `[addr]:port` (brackets only around IPv6) with a plain decimal port from 1024 to 65535 (no sign, no leading zero, no space, no other character); an IPv6 address is in RFC 5952 text, has no zone, is not IPv4-mapped and is not in fe80::/10; the address is not one of the device's own; it lies inside the subnet (address and prefix) of an up, non-tunnel interface address; and lanVerdict(address, that interface address, false) allows it. `target.host` is the address as dialled.

mdnsAnswers.note: mDNS address learning (15.4 Addresses). `packet` is one mDNS response as lower-case hex (header, then the answer and additional sections; names may be compressed, RFC 1035 4.1.4). `source` is the packet's source address as text and `zone` the interface it arrived on (null: none). A browser believes an A or AAAA record only when its address equals `source` (so an A record is never believed in an IPv6 packet, nor an AAAA in an IPv4 packet); the section a record sits in does not matter. A link-local (fe80::/10) address is learned as `<RFC 5952 text>%<zone>`; any other address has no zone. A name keeps at most 4 addresses, of any family, in first-seen order, and a repeat is not a second address. Learning is by that equality alone; there is no address filter at learn time, the dial-time check (15.4.1) decides what may be dialled. `source` may be an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`, or the hex form), which is judged as its IPv4 address: an A record equal to it is learned, an AAAA record never is. An address record with TTL 0 removes that address (the same text, so a link-local address with the same zone) when it passes the same equality test, and learns nothing; records apply in packet order. A PTR goodbye (TTL 0) teaches none and removes none. `prior` (absent: nothing held) is the table the browser held before the packet, in first-seen order; `learned` is the table after it: the `{name, address}` entries in first-seen order. Names compare case-insensitively by ASCII fold (A-Z only) and are held, and shown in `learned`, in lower case. A link-local `source` with `zone` null learns nothing (no arrival interface names the host). The roster filter, the per-source limit on new names and the SRV port range need a roster, a clock and SRV records, which these rows do not model: each SDK tests them itself. Rows need an own DNS codec: Node, Python, Kotlin JVM and Godot GDScript run them; Swift and Android leave address learning to the OS resolver.

vouch.note: Mode v: the vouch (15.6.1). `requests`: M's check of a VOUCH_REQ body, `{id, slug, hHex, hello, body | bodyHex | bodyPad, verdict, close?, result?}`; `hHex` is the session's handshake hash (the mode-v handshake of noise-vectors.json), `hello` the members of D's HELLO, cleaned by 15.6 before they are compared. A refusal closes `peer_bad_frame` and calls no route. The proof is the `vouch` proof of 12.11.1 over `<b64url h>.<request>`. `results`: D's reading of a VOUCH_RESULT body, `{id, body | bodyHex, status | refuse}`. `flows`: the order, direction and gating of rule 7, 8 and 12 on one session, `{id, steps, want}`; a step is an event (`handshake` with both capability lists, `shown`, `picked`, `wrong-pick`, `none-match`, `timeout`, `confirmed`) or a record (`dir` d2m or m2d, `type` as four hex digits: 8010 VOUCH_REQ, 8011 VOUCH_RESULT with its `status`, 0030 to 003f the Sync records with their `bytes`); `want` is the close code the receiving side sends and the step index it closes at, and the indices of the records handed to the host in order. `finish`: what M does with the answer to nearby/approve, `{id, keysRetried, http, body, discoveryNearby, result}` with `result` one of `{send}`, `{wait}` or `{close, stopAdvert}`; a problem body names its refusal in `code`.

A 200 whose body is not JSON: close.

contact.note: Inter-account links (15.10, 15.7 contact rooms, 15.4 the contact advert). `secrets` (the row real-pairing-inputs uses the handshake hash of noise-vectors.json mode-p and the nonces of the sas row p-0): the contact secret, HKDF-SHA256(salt = h, ikm = nD || nM, info = 'pkey-peer/1 contact' || 0x00 || lo || hi), 32 bytes, with h, nD, nM in lower-case hex and the two agreeKeys in the 43-character wire spelling; lo and hi are the 32 raw key bytes by unsigned byte order, so swapping the keys changes nothing and the order is not that of the text. `bodies`: a CONTACT body, `{id, body | bodyHex | bodyPad, length, own?, want}`; `want` is `{ok:false}` or `{ok, agreeKey, label?, cats}`; `own` is the reader's own agreeKey (an equal one refuses). `categories`: a link's categories, the entries both lists hold, once each, in byte order. `exchange`: one side's pairing events in order, `{id, own, steps, want}`; a step is own-confirm, peer-confirm, peer-contact (with its `body` text) or timeout (30 s after this side's CONFIRM, with no CONTACT read yet); `want` has one entry per step with what that step makes this side send (`CONFIRM`, `CONTACT`), the code it closes with, and the contact it stores; after a close nothing more happens. `held` lists the agreeKey of every active contact the host holds: a peer in it is a re-pair and `stored.pending` is true, at any count; a peer not in it is stored (`pending` false) unless 64 are held, when the side closes `peer_not_allowed` at the CONTACT and stores nothing; a body that breaks the rules is `peer_bad_frame` first. `adverts`: `names` (the instance p1- and the first 16 characters of the lower-case base32 of HMAC-SHA256(secret, 'pkey-peer/1 cdisc' || 0x00 || u64be(epoch) || the advertiser's 32 agreeKey bytes)), `txt` (parseContactTxt: v=1 and m=c, no h) and `browse` (which held contact an instance belongs to, in the current or previous epoch, among the first 72 secrets: the held contacts in held order, then the pending ones). `store`: the contact list with pending contacts (15.10): keys and secrets are small integers n, the 32 bytes all equal to n; `start` is the held contacts as [key, secret]; `ops` are pair (a pairing result: a new peer is active, or refused when 64 are held; a held peer is stored pending, one pending per key, at most 8, the oldest goes), promote (a handshake under a pending secret passed the pin: it replaces the held contact of its key in place) and drop (pending contacts stored 86400 s ago or earlier go); `want` is, per op, the result of a pair, the secrets held in order, the pending secrets in the order stored, and `order`, the held then the pending, at most 72, which is the order a responder tries secrets and a browser tests names. `listener`: the shared listener's trial of message 1 (15.5, 15.10): `account` lists the discKeys (null = none; only the first two are tried) or is null for a host without an account; `contacts` lists the secrets in `order`; `opens` names the one key whose tag verifies; `limiter` is what the contact-trial limiter says; `want.tried` is every key a tag was tried under in order (`a:<i>` account key, `c:<i>` contact), `hit` the key that decided, `slot` whether the connection still holds a limiter slot after message 1 (a contact hit holds it until message 3; a refused or failed trial holds none) and `close` the silent end (`peer_busy` when the limiter refused before any contact secret was tried, `handshake_failed` when no tag verified). `pin`: the remote static key against the agreeKey of the contact whose secret opened the session: a mismatch is `peer_revoked` and nothing is sent; the initiator checks after message 2, the responder after message 3. `rooms`: `rid` (base64url of the first 16 bytes of HKDF-SHA256(salt empty, ikm secret, info 'pkey-peer/1 room')) and `alias` (the first 24 bytes of SHA-256(rid bytes || deviceId bytes) as 48 hex characters; rid is its 16 decoded bytes and deviceId its 24). `tickets`: the contact ticket-request body, strict JSON of at most 256 bytes with exactly `room` = 'c' and a canonical 22-character `rid`. Append-only: a new row keeps peerMatrixVersion; a changed row or rule bumps it.

xfer.note: Direct Transfer, xfer/1 (15.11). Constants: control body at most 4096 bytes, size at most 2^40, default chunk 61440, largest chunk 65492, window 16 chunks, an ACK at least every 8 chunks, 4 live transfers per session, consent 120 s, idle 60 s, a partial lives 86400 s, 8 partials per peer, the last 64 ended ids remembered. `codecs`: `offer` (`{id, body | bodyHex, length, maxMessage, want}`; `maxMessage` is the reader's own HELLO value and the chunk plus 24 must fit it; `want` is `{ok:false}` or `{ok, offer}` with only the members present), `offsetBodies` (ACCEPT and ACK `{id, kind, size, chunk, body, want}`; an ACK may equal size, an ACCEPT may not unless it is a multiple of chunk), `done` (`toward` receiver needs a lower-case hex sha256, toward sender must not carry one), `cancel` (a string reason outside the eight reads as cancelled), `chunk` (`{id, size, chunk, expect, head, dataLength, want}`: the body is `head` as hex followed by dataLength bytes of 0xab; `expect` is the next offset the receiver wants). Every `ok:false` is a peer_bad_frame fault. `window`, `offer`, `hash`, `ending`, `resume`, `limits`: one side of a session as a machine, `{id, ctx, steps, want}`; `want` has one entry per step, the output of that step, and after a close nothing more happens. `ctx`: `mode`, `capsLocal` and `capsRemote` (the handshake payload `caps`; the session's are the intersection), `maxMessage` (this side's own HELLO value), `hostLimit` and `free` (bytes, null for none), `handler` (how the host answers an offer: `accept` at once, `ask` later through a `consent` step, `decline`, `none` for no handler), `cats` (the link's categories, mode c), `partials` (kept partial files of this peer key: `{ref, id, sha256, size, chunk, bytes, writtenAt, held?, reread?, corrupt?, otherPeer?}`; `held` a live transfer in another session holds it, `reread` the bytes re-read and hashed since the session began, default `bytes`, `corrupt` its bytes are not the content, `otherPeer` it belongs to another remote key), `peerKey` (hex of the 32 raw bytes) and `withholdAcks` (this receiver has sent no ACK yet, so the window is judged from the accept offset). A step carries `at` (seconds on the row's clock; a wait that ran out by then ends first with CANCEL timeout, and no row stands on the exact edge) and one of: `rx` (a record read: OFFER with its `body` text; ACCEPT and ACK `{id, offset}`; CHUNK `{id, offset, length}` whose data is the transfer's content, `data: corrupt` XORs each byte with 0xff; DONE `{id, sha256?}`; CANCEL `{id, reason}`; PING; `more` sets the MORE flag) or `host` (`offer` starts a send with `{id, size, chunk, sha256, cat?, seekable?}`; `consent` answers the question with `accept` or `decline`; `cancel`; `close` the session ends; `newSession` a new session on the same machine keeps the partials; `tick` only moves the clock). The content of every transfer is byte i = (7 i + 13) mod 256, so each sha256 in a row is the SHA-256 of that content and a CHUNK needs no data in the row. An output holds the keys that apply: `send` (OFFER, ACCEPT, ACK, DONE, CANCEL `{id, reason}`, and CHUNKS `{id, offset, bytes}`, the consecutive CHUNK records one step sends, `chunk` bytes each and the last the remainder), `close` (a peer_* code), `ask` (the host is asked: id, name as shown, type, size, cat), `withdraw` (the question is withdrawn), `result` (`delivered` once the receiver's hash matched or the sender read DONE `{id}`; `cancelled` with its reason; `closed`; reported only for a transfer that reached ACCEPT), `partial` (effects on the kept files: `create`, `truncate` to an offset, `discard`, `evict`, `keep`, `delete`, `finalize`), `refused` (the host's own send was refused locally: busy) and `drop` (a late record for an ended id, without effect). A refusal CANCEL ends that id at once. `name`: `paths` (`{id, key, xferId, sha256, path}`: hex of SHA-256('pkey-xfer/1 partial' || 0x00 || key || idBytes || sha256Bytes), key 32 raw bytes, id 16 decoded bytes, sha256 32 decoded bytes) and `rows` (an OFFER `body` whose name is a path-like string: the path of its partial file is the same for all, `display` is the name as shown, the §12.7.1 cleaning without the 64 code point cut, null when nothing is left, and `type` is passed on as given and never used). Append-only: a new row keeps peerMatrixVersion; a changed row or rule bumps it.

local.note: Account-free local pairing (15.12, 15.4, 15.5). `codes`: `nameplate` (a byte stream drawn one byte at a time: 200 or more is drawn again, then mod 100; a nameplate in `inUse` is drawn again unless all 100 are in use; `want.consumed` is the bytes read and a null nameplate means the stream ran out), `password` (4 bytes a draw as a u32be, drawn again at 4294000000 or more, then mod 10^6, written with leading zeros), `display` (two groups of four digits, one space) and `parse` (a typed code: ASCII spaces and hyphens removed, then exactly 8 ASCII digits; nothing else, another script's digits included). `qr`: `make` (PKP1:SLUG:INSTANCE:SECRET in upper case, the instance's 16 base32 characters and the secret's 26 with the two unused low bits zero) and `parse` (fold ASCII case, four fields split at ':', then ok, other-app when the slug is well formed but not `own`, or invalid; the secret's last character must keep its low two bits zero). `adverts`: `pairing` (the m=q instance p1- + the 16 base32 characters of the window's 10 bytes), `names` (the m=l instance p1- + the first 16 characters of the lower-case base32 of HMAC-SHA256(secret, 'pkey-peer/1 ldisc' || 0x00 || u64be(epoch) || the advertiser's own link key)) and `browse` (which held link, in held order and among the first 32, an instance belongs to in the current or previous epoch; each link lists its `secret` and the peer's link key `peerKey`, the key the peer advertises with). `txt`: `parser` txt is parseTxt (m = a, v, p or q; for q `h` is 16 lower-case hex characters and `n` exactly two ASCII digits; n is read for q only; c and l are unknown modes there), `parser` local is parseLocalTxt (v=1 and m=l; no h and no n are read); an entry splits at its first '='; one without '=' or with an empty key is ignored; a repeated key refuses. `body`: a LOCAL_LINK body, strict JSON of at most 4 KiB, v = 1, an optional label cleaned as a HELLO label (nothing left means none), cats an array of at most 8 distinct strings of ^[a-z0-9-]{1,32}$; unknown members are ignored. `secrets`: HKDF-SHA256(salt = h, ikm = ISK (64 bytes), info = 'pkey-peer/1 local' || 0x00 || lo || hi), 32 bytes, lo and hi the two link public keys by unsigned byte order (the row real-pairing-inputs uses the mode-q handshake of noise-vectors.json `cpace.handshakes`). `handshakePayloads`: the payloads of modes q and l and the capability negotiation. `exchange`: one side's pairing events in order (own-confirm, own-decline, peer-confirm, peer-link with the body text, timeout-confirm: the 120 s from the first byte ran out, timeout-exchange: the 30 s after both CONFIRMs ran out), with `held` the local links the device holds and `cats` this side's approved categories; `want` has one entry per step: what that step makes this side send (CONFIRM, LOCAL_LINK, the second once this side's CONFIRM is sent and the peer's read), the code it closes with, and the link it stores (`label`, and `cats` the entries both sides listed in byte order, then peer_bye); after a close nothing more happens; a decline before this side's CONFIRM closes peer_bye. `pin`: mode l checks the remote static key against the peer link key of the link whose secret opened the session (after message 2 for the initiator, after message 3 for the responder): a mismatch is peer_revoked and nothing is sent; mode q ends the handshake silently when the remote static key is this side's own link key. `trialOrder`: the shared listener's trial of message 1: account discKeys (null = none; two tried), then contact secrets (72 tried), then local-link secrets (32 tried), at most 104 secrets after the account keys; `opens` names the key whose tag verifies; `limiter` is what the contact limiter says to a contact or local-link trial; `want.tried` lists a:<i>, c:<i> and l:<i> in order, `hit` the key that decided, `slot` whether the connection holds a limiter slot until message 3 (a contact or local-link hit), `close` the silent end (peer_busy when the limiter refused before any secret was tried, handshake_failed otherwise). `window`: the pairing window's machine over events with a monotonic time t in seconds (open, c1 with `valid`, msg1 with `opens`, abandon, session-end with `stored`, tick, close); `want` has one entry per event: `result` (opened, already-open, closed, busy, limited, refused, attempt, transport, failed, too-many-tries), `open`, `holder` (attempt from a valid C1 until its message 1 or 30 s; session from a message 1 that opens until it ends), `failures`, `rotations` (the password and QR secret rotate after every failed guess below the fifth and after a session that ends without a link while the window is open), `closed` (expired at 300 s, too-many-tries, stored, person) and `host`; a window admits at most 5 C1s in any 60 s, counted when it admits them. `join`: the joiner: `input` is what the reader said (a code's nameplate, a QR's instance or invalid), `adverts` the m=q adverts seen in first-seen order (`h` current, previous or other, `n` the nameplate), `dials` how each dial ends (transport, before-c2, after-c2); `want` has the instances kept (matching h and the nameplate or the instance, at most 8, once each), those dialled (at most 2, in order), whether anything was browsed, and the result: transport, pairing-code-failed (an invalid input, or no transport and an attempt failed after C2) or pairing-not-found. `gate`: the cached discovery answer (`start` on, off or none) over reads (ok with the discovery body, not-found, error) and calls; services.connect.localPairing is true only as the boolean true; an ok read replaces the answer, a not-found clears it, an error changes nothing; a read that leaves a cached true behind has the effects close-windows, withdraw-adverts and end-sessions; a call that opens, joins, advertises, browses, dials or answers needs on and otherwise answers local-pairing-off, and list, rename, remove and set-reachable are never gated. `records`: the mode rules of 15.6 for q and l (and the new rows in the other modes): a known type in a mode that does not allow it closes peer_not_allowed, an unknown type with the critical bit closes peer_unknown_critical and any other is ignored; `needs` is the capability the session must hold. Append-only: a new row keeps peerMatrixVersion; a changed row or rule bumps it.

handshakePayloads.note: Handshake payloads of modes q and l (15.5, 15.12): the rules of a non-account mode, strict JSON of at most 8 KiB, an object; message 1 needs v = 1 (the integer token) and no cert; messages 2 and 3 need v = 1 and caps (at most 32 entries matching ^[a-z0-9]+/[0-9]+$); a cert refuses; ring and unknown members are ignored. `negotiate`: the session's capabilities, the entries both lists hold, once each, in byte order; in mode q a side whose capabilities lack local/1 closes peer_not_allowed after HELLO, before any consent prompt; mode l has no mandatory capability.
